metaDescription: Six juicers built for lower noise, from slow cold press auger models to a compact centrifugal and a citrus press, compared on motor, chute and cleanup.
expertTake: The Canoly C16 cold press is the best overall pick because a slow auger and a brushless motor are the mechanism behind a quiet juicer, and it adds a wide chute. The Eurolux citrus press is the value pick if oranges and lemons are all you juice. Anyone who wants juice in thirty seconds from hard carrots should accept a louder centrifugal machine instead.
introParagraphs: Noise in a juicer comes from how fast the part that breaks down the produce is spinning. A basket that whirls at thousands of revolutions per minute is loud, while an auger that turns at a slow crawl is far quieter, which is why slow juicers dominate the low-noise end of the category.

Quiet is only one trade. Slower machines take longer per glass, have more parts to clean and often cost more, so the right pick depends on how often you juice and what you put in. This guide explains the mechanisms, decodes the claims on the box and ranks six machines by who they suit.

products.name: Canoly C16 3-in-1 Cold Press Juicer 6-Inch Chute AC Brushless
products.description:
The Canoly C16 is a slow masticating juicer with an AC brushless motor that the maker says runs at a whisper-quiet 35 dB. A 6 inch feed chute takes whole apples, which cuts the chopping that makes slow juicers a chore, and two strainers let it make juice or frozen-fruit sorbet. The decibel figure is the maker's own claim and no measurement distance is given, but the slow auger is the real source of the low noise.

The tradeoff is time and cleanup. A slow juicer takes noticeably longer per glass than a centrifugal machine, and the auger, strainers and brush need washing after every use. Compared with the Breville Juice Fountain it is quieter in principle but far slower, and next to the CELVARA it is a near twin in format with a more specific noise statement.

Ownership is simple if you rinse the strainer right after juicing, because dried pulp in a fine mesh is the thing that ends juicers. Use the supplied brush, avoid hard frozen chunks in the juice strainer and keep the silicone seals in good condition.
products.bestFor: Households juicing most mornings who want low noise and little chopping.
pros: Slow auger is the quietest mechanism
cons: Several parts to wash after each use
Noise figure is a maker claim

products.name: CELVARA 3-in-1 Cold Press Juicer 6.5-Inch Feed Chute
products.description:
The CELVARA offers the widest feed chute here at 6.5 inches, driven by an AC brushless motor and a large auger. The maker claims it handles ten pounds of carrots in a few minutes, which suggests the auger is sized for volume, and the interchangeable strainers cover juice and sorbet. A wide chute saves roughly half the prep time because whole fruit goes in.

The tradeoff is bulk and brand history. A wide chute and large auger make a tall, heavy machine that needs counter space, and newer brands have thinner track records than Ninja or Breville. Compared with the Canoly it has a slightly wider chute but no published decibel figure.

Wash it immediately after use, soak the strainer in warm water and use the brush. Check the seals and replace worn ones before leaks start.
products.bestFor: Juicing large batches of whole produce with minimal prep.
pros: 6.5 inch chute is the widest here

products.name: Ninja NeverClog JC151 Cold Press Juicer 24 oz Jug
products.description:
The Ninja NeverClog uses a 150W high-torque auger, two pulp filters for less or more pulp and a reverse function that backs out jams. A 24 ounce jug and a 36 ounce pulp bin let it run non-stop for a while before you have to empty it. The slow auger is the reason it is quieter than a centrifugal machine, even without a published decibel number.

The tradeoff is that its chute is narrower than the Canoly and CELVARA, so more chopping is needed. Compared with the Breville it is slower but yields drier pulp and handles leafy greens better.

Rinse the parts at once, use the brush on the strainer and let everything dry before storing. The reverse button is for jams, not for routine use.
products.bestFor: People juicing fibrous vegetables and greens who want jam protection.
pros: Large pulp bin for long runs
cons: Narrower chute than the 6 inch models

products.name: Breville BJE200XL Juice Fountain Compact Centrifugal Juicer
products.description:
The Breville Juice Fountain Compact is a centrifugal juicer with a 3 inch chute, a titanium reinforced disc and an Italian-made micro mesh filter. Its listing says it juices whole produce quietly, which is relative: it is quieter than larger centrifugal machines but louder than a slow auger. Speed is the draw, with a glass of juice in under a minute.

The tradeoff is that centrifugal juicers shred at high RPM, which creates more foam, more heat and more noise than a cold press. Against the Canoly it is far faster but noticeably louder, and against the BLACK+DECKER it is a better-built machine.

Clean the filter right after use, because pulp dries in mesh quickly. Run it in short bursts, since budget centrifugal units are meant for a minute or two of continuous running per batch.
products.bestFor: People who want fast juice and accept a moderate noise level.
pros: Fast, under a minute per glass

products.name: BLACK+DECKER JE2500B Quiet Fruit and Vegetable Juicer
products.description:
The BLACK+DECKER JE2500B is sold as a quiet fruit and vegetable juicer, with a twist assembly, a non-drip spout and dishwasher-safe parts. The maker promises fast juicing with less noise, which is a relative claim made against the maker's own earlier models rather than against a cold press juicer.

The tradeoff is that it is still a centrifugal machine, so it cannot match the quiet of a slow auger. Against the Breville it is simpler and cheaper but less robust, and against the Canoly it is faster but louder.

Use it in short batches, rinse the filter right away and keep the parts out of the dishwasher heat if the manual warns against it. Because the spout twists shut, wipe it dry before storing so that old juice does not sour inside the mechanism, and expect the plastic filter basket to stain from carrot and beet over time without affecting performance.
products.bestFor: Occasional juicing where cost and easy assembly matter.

products.name: Eurolux Electric Citrus Juicer 300W 110 RPM One-Touch
products.description:
The Eurolux is an electric citrus juicer with a 300W motor that turns a reamer at 110 RPM, which is slow enough to be quiet. One-touch operation lets you press a halved orange against the cone and let it spin. It handles oranges, lemons and grapefruit only.

The tradeoff is scope. It cannot juice carrots, greens or apples, so it is not a general juicer. Compared with the Canoly it is far cheaper and simpler but does only one family of fruit.

Wash the cone and bowl after each use and keep the body dry. A stainless body wipes clean easily.
products.bestFor: Citrus drinkers who want a quiet daily orange juice machine.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A centrifugal juicer spins a shredding basket at thousands of revolutions per minute, and the whine of that basket plus the impact of produce on the disc is the main source of noise. A masticating juicer turns an auger at roughly 40 to 100 RPM, so there is no high-speed whirl. That is why the Canoly, CELVARA and Ninja are quieter in principle than the Breville and BLACK+DECKER. The decibel numbers on boxes are maker claims, usually measured at an unstated distance, so use the mechanism as your guide rather than the figure. Expect a slow juicer to hum and crunch rather than scream.

A narrow chute forces you to cut produce into sticks, and the extra prep time is the main reason slow juicers end up in cupboards. The Canoly offers 6 inches, the CELVARA 6.5 inches and the Breville 3 inches. A wide chute takes whole apples and large carrots, so you juice faster. The tradeoff is a taller, heavier machine and a bigger hopper to clean. Choose by how much chopping you will tolerate on a weekday morning, not by the biggest number.

Slow juicers yield about 10 to 30 percent more juice from leafy greens than centrifugal machines, and the pulp comes out drier. A centrifugal juicer such as the Breville is very good with hard fruit and carrots but wastes more with kale and herbs. Check whether the machine has a pulp filter or adjustable outlet, as on the Ninja, which gives control over pulp. If you juice greens often, a masticating machine will repay its extra cost within a few months of produce savings.

Cleanup time is the biggest reason juicers are abandoned. Count the parts that touch juice: the strainer, the auger, the chamber, the lid, the pulp bin and the brush. Dishwasher-safe parts, as on the BLACK+DECKER, help, but fine mesh should still be brushed. Rinse everything within minutes of juicing, because dried pulp in a mesh screen is nearly impossible to remove. A machine with fewer pieces, like the Eurolux citrus press, is the easiest.

Brushless AC motors, as in the Canoly and CELVARA, run cooler and last longer than brushed motors. Budget centrifugal units are meant for one to two minutes of continuous running per batch, then a rest. Slow juicers can run longer but should still be given short breaks on hard vegetables. A reverse function, as on the Ninja, clears jams safely. Never force produce down with anything but the supplied pusher.

Match the machine to your produce. If you drink orange juice every morning, a citrus press like the Eurolux is quiet, cheap and fast. If you juice carrots, apples and greens, a slow juicer is better. If you want a quick glass from hard fruit and accept more noise, a centrifugal unit works. Buying a machine for a use you will not repeat is the most common juicer mistake and the main reason used ones fill online marketplaces.

specDecoder.meaning: A slow auger that crushes produce. It is quieter and yields more from greens.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Canoly, CELVARA and Ninja are masticating.

specDecoder.meaning: A fast spinning basket that shreds produce. It is faster and louder.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Breville and BLACK+DECKER are centrifugal.

specDecoder.meaning: The opening width. A wide chute reduces chopping.

A function that runs the auger backward to clear jams.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise mechanism
howWeEvaluated.description: We judged noise by the mechanism rather than the published number. Slow augers and slow reamers scored highest. A claim such as 35 dB was treated as a claim. We also noted that maker statements about quiet operation are relative and not measured against a shared standard.

howWeEvaluated.title: Juicing capability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared chute width, motor type and strainer design from the listings. The widest chutes reduce prep time. Machines that handle both fruit and greens scored higher than citrus-only presses. Real yields vary with produce and technique.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleanup
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted parts, noted dishwasher-safe components and considered how easily the strainer can be brushed. Fewer parts earned more points. Machines with fine mesh and many pieces lost points. Owner feedback patterns repeatedly show that cleanup decides how long a juicer stays in use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Durability
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at motor type, duty cycle and replaceable parts. Brushless motors and reverse functions scored higher. Newer brands lost points for limited history. Short duty cycles on centrifugal units were treated as a limit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit and value
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each juicer to a likely user, such as a citrus drinker or a green juicer. We considered the lineup's spread of format, from a citrus press to a wide chute cold press. Scores are based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns.

cards.label: Slow juicing
cards.text: The Canoly, CELVARA and Ninja crush produce with an auger. They are quieter, give drier pulp and handle greens well, but each glass takes longer.

cards.label: Fast juicing
cards.text: The Breville and BLACK+DECKER shred produce on a spinning basket. They are quick and need less prep with a wide chute, but they are louder and foamier.

howToChoose.note: Choose slow for quiet and greens, and fast for speed on hard produce.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a slow auger or a slow reamer, a wide chute so you can skip chopping and parts that rinse in a minute. Avoid a high-speed basket if you juice before the household wakes.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Canoly C16 is the best match for general juicing and the Eurolux for citrus. The Ninja is the best choice for fibrous vegetables because it clears jams.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you juice daily or juice greens, where a cold press such as the Canoly or Ninja earns its cost through yield and low noise.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you juice occasionally. The Eurolux for citrus or the BLACK+DECKER for general use is enough.

maintenance.why: Dried pulp in fine mesh is very hard to remove. Rinsing within a few minutes keeps the strainer working.
The brush clears the micro mesh that a rinse alone leaves clogged. Use the supplied brush instead of a hard scrubber.
Worn silicone seals leak juice into the motor housing. Replace them as soon as they harden or crack.
Carrot and beet staining and hard water can build up. A warm soak keeps the parts clear.
The lid must latch for the machine to run. Sensors can fail over time, so test the lock before relying on it.

faq.a: Yes, in general. An auger turning at a low speed makes far less noise than a basket spinning thousands of times per minute. Published decibel claims are not standardized, so judge by the mechanism. Expect a hum and a crunch instead of a whine.

faq.q: Is a centrifugal juicer ever quiet?
faq.a: Some are marketed as quiet, and the BLACK+DECKER and Breville describe lower noise. That is relative to other centrifugal juicers. They remain louder than a slow juicer. If noise is your main concern, a cold press is the safer pick.

faq.q: Do slow juicers take much longer?
faq.a: They take longer per glass, often several minutes for a full batch. A wide chute cuts prep time. If you juice daily, the extra minutes are usually acceptable for better yield and lower noise.

faq.q: Can a cold press juicer handle hard carrots?
faq.a: Yes, and it is one of their strengths. A high-torque auger crushes carrots and beets well. Cut very large pieces if your chute is narrow and use the reverse function if the machine jams.
Only if you juice citrus. A reamer cannot handle carrots, apples or greens. For general juicing choose a cold press or centrifugal juicer.

faq.q: How do I keep it from clogging?
faq.a: Cut produce into suitable sizes, alternate soft and hard items and rinse the strainer promptly. Use reverse on jams. Do not push produce with anything but the supplied pusher.
